nodes.label: Scaling is three questions: code, instances, data
nodes.rationale: Interviewers rarely say which of the three they mean, and the order matters. Kubernetes multiplies instances; it cannot make un-scalable code scalable. The senior closer is refusing to touch any layer before knowing which one is actually the problem — most 'we need to scale' turns out to be one N+1 query.

nodes.label: Thread-pool starvation from sync-over-async
nodes.rationale: Measured with 100 virtual users for 10 s on a 4-core VM: async 979.0 RPS with a 105.4 ms p99 against sync-over-async 35.2 RPS with a 3530.7 ms p99 — 27.8x throughput and 33.5x lower p99 with zero infrastructure change. .Result blocks a pool thread for the whole wait and the pool grows by only one or two threads per second, so 96 of 100 requests queue for a thread rather than for the database. Matching it would take ~28 instances.

nodes.label: What stateless actually means
nodes.rationale: Not 'has no state' but 'no state that matters lives in the process'. Static dictionaries, in-memory semaphores, sessions, rate-limit counters, in-process job schedulers and SignalR groups all break at more than one instance; databases, row and advisory locks, distributed caches, queues with leader election and a SignalR Redis backplane survive. Spotting the same failure across unrelated technologies is what the interview question is really testing.

nodes.label: SignalR groups are per-process (ContentionHub)
nodes.rationale: This repo has the bug on purpose: at three replicas a client connected to instance 2 misses events published on instance 1, because SignalR groups live in process memory. Same class of failure as the in-memory lock in a different costume; the fix is a Redis backplane.

nodes.label: Idempotency keys for repeated operations
nodes.rationale: Concurrency safety does not make a repeated operation safe. Five retries applied five times leave a balance of 500 against an expected 900 — every retry individually correct and concurrency-safe, the customer still charged five times. The guarantee must come from a uniqueness constraint in the database: checking 'have I seen this key?' then inserting is the read-modify-write race wearing a different hat.

nodes.label: The costs of scaling out
nodes.rationale: Every replica multiplies database load; coordination gets slower (the distributed lock took ~2.6 s of total waiting where the in-process semaphore took ~8 ms — correctness across instances costs a round-trip per acquire); debugging needs correlation ids and aggregated logging; stateless costs infrastructure (Redis, backplane, queue with leader election). Vertical scaling is underrated: a bigger machine is often cheaper and always simpler.

hyperedges.label: The coordination point must live in shared state, not process memory
